items.title: DeepSeek Harness Stunningly Open-Sourced Now: Everything Becomes a Plugin - 36Kr
items.summary_1line: DeepSeek Harness Stunningly Open-Sourced Now: Everything Becomes a Plugin 36Kr
items.editor_note: 36Kr's Chinese-press confirmation that Harness is now open source, a day after the initial launch coverage.

editorial.tldr: DeepSeek was spotted testing an agent harness in early August, alongside the cheap V4 model that had already jolted Silicon Valley on price. Ten days later it open sourced that harness outright, pairing the release with a pricier V4-Pro API tier.
editorial.whats_new: Chinese outlet 36Kr now confirms the open source Harness release a day after the VentureBeat/New Stack launch coverage, signaling the framework is drawing attention in both the US and Chinese press.
editorial.why_it_matters: An open, inspectable agent harness from a low-cost model lab gives platform engineers a second reference architecture to compare against Claude Code, but the accompanying V4-Pro price increase changes the cost math that made DeepSeek attractive in the first place.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before treating DeepSeek Harness as a Claude Code substitute, check whether its plugin interface covers your current tool-calling and memory setup, and re-run your cost comparison against V4-Pro's new, higher API price.

beats.summary: DeepSeek formalized the release as a plugin-based framework and raised API pricing for the paired V4-Pro model; 36Kr's Aug 14 coverage confirms the open-source launch landed in the Chinese press too.

open_questions: Does Harness's plugin interface match or diverge from Claude Code's tool-calling conventions, and how much rework would porting an existing agent take?
How does V4-Pro's higher API price compare on a cost-per-task basis against base V4 and against Claude Code once agent overhead is factored in?
Will independent benchmarks test Harness's plugin architecture against established agent frameworks, or is this still framework-only with no eval data?
